# Act, review, or escalate {#sec-ch14}

::: {.epigraph by="Sign on President Harry S. Truman's desk"}
The buck stops here.
:::

An alert comes in at 2 a.m. The model says 0.37. You know it's a probability and how to check it. Now someone on the team asks the only question that matters: *"So what do we do with it?"* Close it? Queue it for the morning? Wake someone up?

This chapter is that step, from a number to an action. It's the least exciting part of any AI system, and it's where most of the money is saved or lost.

::: {.goals}
- Explain why a single threshold at 0.5 is almost always the wrong policy.
- Split decisions into three zones (act, review, escalate) and say what each zone *means* in a real team.
- Work out the zone thresholds from what mistakes cost, then adjust them for how many people you actually have.
- Check calibration before trusting any threshold, and fix it when it's off.
- Run the policy in real use: decision logs, fail-safes, audits, and drift.
:::

## The obvious answer

Every tutorial says: above 0.5, it's a threat; below, it's fine. Try it on a realistic week: three weeks of history, then a fourth week treated as live.

About {{< num ch21 naive.act int >}} alerts a day close themselves. Wonderful, until the next line: every day, about {{< num ch21 naive.missed_by_automation int >}} of them were real threats (real phishing, real malware, a real stranger with someone's password) closed with nobody looking.

0.5 quietly assumes two false things: that a missed threat and a false alarm cost the same, and that there are only two things you can do with an alert. There are three.

## Three doors

Every alert leaves through one of three doors. The quiet door: it's closed automatically and nobody reads it; most alerts should go this way. The queue: a person reads the logs and decides, about twelve minutes of skilled time. The loud door: someone's phone rings, at 2 a.m. if necessary, because this one can't wait.

::: {.keyidea}
Act, review, escalate: machines handle the clear cases at each end, and people handle the middle.
:::

**Act**: the system handles it alone. **Review**: a person checks it in normal work. **Escalate**: a person is called in now. The names are general on purpose. In customer support: automatic reply, human agent, supervisor. In content moderation: auto-approve, human review, legal team.

![420 alerts from the live week, placed by how likely the (calibrated) model thinks they are to be real threats. Note the log scale: most alerts are crowded at the far left, where the model is confident they're harmless. The red crosses, real threats, are mostly to the right, but not all of them.](/figures/ch21/zones-strip.pdf){#fig-zones-strip}

The whole problem is in @fig-zones-strip. Harmless alerts crowd the left; real threats sit mostly to the right, but some are scattered through the middle and a few hide in the harmless crowd. No two thresholds put every dot in the right zone. The job is to make the *unavoidable* mistakes the cheap ones.

## Let the costs set the thresholds

For each action, write down what it costs *on average*, given the probability *P* that the alert is real. These are my estimates for a mid-sized company, not industry figures; the method matters more than the values.

- **Act** (auto-close). If the alert was real, we've let a threat through. Other defences catch much of what gets past, so the *expected* loss per missed threat is about \$10,000. Expected cost: *P* × \$10,000.
- **Review.** Twelve minutes of an analyst's time at \$75 an hour is \$15. Analysts are human and miss about one threat in twenty. Expected cost: \$15 + *P* × 5% × \$10,000.
- **Escalate** (call the analyst on call). If the alert was harmless, we've woken someone up for nothing. Call that \$400. Expected cost: (1 − *P*) × \$400.

Now draw all three as lines against *P*. At every value of *P*, pick the cheapest one.

![Expected cost of each action as the probability of a real threat rises (both axes on a log scale). Acting is cheapest when P is tiny, escalating when P is large, and review wins everywhere in between. The two crossing points are the thresholds.](/figures/ch21/cost-lines.pdf){#fig-cost-lines}

The two crossings in @fig-cost-lines are your thresholds, and a pencil finds them. Acting beats reviewing when *P* × 10,000 < 15 + *P* × 500: *P* below about 0.0016. Escalating beats reviewing above about 0.43.

Look at that first number again. The machine may close an alert alone only if it's *99.8% sure* it's harmless. That's not paranoia; it's arithmetic. An unseen real threat costs about 630 times a review.

::: {.threshold}
Suppose the company buys better protection for its laptops and servers, and the expected loss from a missed threat falls from \$10,000 to \$2,000. Work out the *act* threshold again with the same formula: 15 ÷ (2,000 × 0.95). Does it move up or down? By about how much? What happens to the number of alerts the machine can close alone?

(It moves up, to about 0.008, five times higher, so far more alerts can safely close themselves. When misses cost less, you can automate more.)
:::

## Before you trust a threshold, check the probability

Those cost lines assume *P* means what it says. If the model says 0.001 when the truth is 0.003, your "cheapest action" isn't, and the machine closes threats you never agreed to close.

So check first. Among live alerts the raw model called "under 2% likely", it said {{< num ch21 raw_believed pct1 >}} on average; the real rate was {{< num ch21 raw_actual pct1 >}}. Its "almost certainly harmless" alerts were {{< num ch21 raw_ratio f1 >}} times riskier than claimed. The stand-in model is built slightly overconfident at the extremes, as most real models are (Chapter 5). Never assume either way for *your* model on *your* data; measure it (Chapter 11).

![A close-up of the low end, where the act zone is. Raw scores (red, solid line) sit above the diagonal: the model was more confident than it should have been. After Platt scaling fitted on other days (green, dashed line), the curve stays much closer to the diagonal.](/figures/ch21/calibration-zones.pdf){#fig-calibration-zones}

After Platt scaling, fitted only on the three history weeks, the picture improves (@fig-calibration-zones). It's not perfect, but it's much closer. So here is the rule, stated properly:

::: {.keyidea}
Never put a threshold on a probability you haven't checked against recent outcomes.
:::

From here on, every threshold we set is on the *calibrated* probabilities.

## Then the real limit appears: the queue

Switch the cost-based policy on, and it sends about {{< num ch21 ideal.review int >}} alerts a day to review: a full day's work for about {{< num ch21 ideal_reviews_analysts int >}} people. The team has {{< num ch21 analysts int >}}. At about 40 alerts a shift each, the queue can take {{< num ch21 capacity int >}} a day, and the on-call person can take about {{< num ch21 pages_cap int >}} urgent calls.

::: {.keyidea}
A policy that ignores capacity isn't a policy. It's a wish.
:::

Anything beyond {{< num ch21 capacity int >}} simply doesn't get looked at, and nobody chooses which ones are skipped.

So ask a better question: *among policies that fit the team we actually have, which is cheapest?* (For any escalate threshold, the best act threshold is the one that just fills the queue.) Fitted on history and checked on the live week, the machine now closes about {{< num ch21 chosen.act int >}} alerts a day by itself. The analysts get {{< num ch21 chosen.review int >}}, and the analyst on call gets {{< num ch21 chosen.escalate int >}} urgent calls. The number of real threats closed without a person falls from {{< num ch21 naive.missed_by_automation int >}} a day to about {{< num ch21 chosen.missed_by_automation f1 >}}.

The live week slightly overfills the team ({{< num ch21 chosen.review int >}} reviews against {{< num ch21 capacity int >}}). Expect that: thresholds fitted on the past are a forecast, not a promise. Watch the queue every day.

![Where the live week's real threats (left) and harmless alerts (right) end up each day, under one threshold at 0.5 and under the three-zone policy that respects capacity. The light, plain segment on the left (act) is the number that matters: threats closed with no person involved.](/figures/ch21/one-vs-three.pdf){#fig-one-vs-three}

In @fig-one-vs-three, the harmless alerts the machine closes barely change. The threats it closes unseen go from the biggest segment to the smallest. But about six a day still isn't zero. Now think like the person who approves the budget.

![Threats auto-closed per day, for every team size from 3 to 14 analysts, with thresholds fitted again for each. The gap between the two curves is what better input is worth: the same model reading structured alert fields instead of raw alert text.](/figures/ch21/capacity.pdf){#fig-capacity}

@fig-capacity is the chapter's most useful chart. Each point is the best policy for that team size. Going from six people to eight cuts unseen threats from {{< num ch21 chosen.missed_by_automation f1 >}} a day to {{< num ch21 eight.missed_by_automation f1 >}}, avoiding about {{< num ch21 saved_money_per_day money >}} of expected loss a day. The model doesn't make that call, and neither do you alone. But it's now a decision with a clear price, not a guess.

The grey curve is the same model reading raw text instead of clean fields: worse at every team size. *Better input buys the same as more people.* That's the idea behind "the LLM extracts, the decision model decides" (Chapter 15).

::: {.keyidea}
Capacity is part of the policy: the right thresholds depend on how many people you have.
:::

::: {.sidebar title="Why not just maximise accuracy?"}
Because accuracy counts every mistake as one mistake. When 8% of alerts are real, closing everything is 92% accurate, and a disaster. Costs and capacity are what turn "a good model" into "a good decision".
:::

## When the answer has more than two options

Real triage asks several questions at once: is it real, what kind, how severe? With several answers, the policy needs one more rule that people often forget.

::: {.keyidea}
Stakes override confidence.
:::

A model can be 99% sure an alert on the payroll server is harmless, but the other 1% is still on the payroll server. So the policy weighs *what's at risk* as well as *how likely*. Two rules worth copying: nothing on a critical system closes itself, however confident the model; and anything that doesn't clearly belong behind another door goes to a person. *When in doubt, review.*

For a pick-one question like "which team?", act on the top label only when its probability clears your threshold, and review the rest.

## Running it for real

A policy that works on paper is a third of the job. The rest is the day the model stops working, the week attackers change methods, and the month an auditor asks why an alert was closed.

![The decision loop in real use. Every alert flows through the model, calibration and a versioned policy into one of three doors. Every decision is logged. Outcomes, including a random audit of alerts the machine closed on its own, come back as labels, and a weekly check decides whether calibration or thresholds need to move.](/figures/ch21/production-loop.pdf){#fig-production-loop}

@fig-production-loop shows the loop. Four habits make it reliable.

**Write the policy down, with a version number.** Thresholds in someone's head change unnoticed. "Policy v3: act below 0.031, escalate at 0.34, fitted on 1–21 September, six people" can be reviewed, tested and rolled back.

**Log every decision.** A decision model gives probabilities, not reasons, but you can make the *system* explainable: record what the model saw, what it said, which policy version turned that into an action, and when.

**When something fails, review, never act.** If the model times out or errors, the case goes to a person. A system must never close cases unseen because something it depends on broke.

**Audit the act zone at random.** The habit teams most often skip, and the one that matters most. Cases sent to people come back with an answer. Cases the machine closed come back with *nothing*, so you never see the machine's own mistakes, in exactly the zone where they hurt. Send a small random share of auto-closed cases, say 3%, to a person anyway. It's the only clear view of the act zone.

::: {.keyidea}
Cases the machine closes never come back with an answer, unless you audit a random sample.
:::

::: {.breaks}
Thresholds are fitted to the past, but attackers act in the future. If an attacker learns what makes your model relax, such as alerts that look like approved IT tools, they will shape their activity to land in the act zone. Three things make this harder: random audits, never showing scores outside the team, and rules that keep critical assets out of the act zone. None make it impossible. The cost figures are guesses too. Check them again when the business changes, not just when the model does.
:::

## The week it broke

Drift, when it arrives, looks like this. In week five, a phishing campaign hits. Alerts about links fire three times as often as usual, and far more of them are real. Nothing about any single alert looks unusual. The model scores them just as it scored last month's.

![Top: the share of alerts that were real threats each day (black, solid line) against what the calibrated model expected (green, dashed line). Bottom: alerts sent to review each day against the team's capacity. In week five (shaded, between dotted lines), reality moves away from the model, and the queue overflows.](/figures/ch21/drift-watch.pdf){#fig-drift-watch}

@fig-drift-watch shows two things going wrong at once. The model expected about {{< num ch21 campaign_pred pct >}} of alerts to be threats; the real figure was {{< num ch21 campaign_actual pct >}}. And the review queue rose to an average of about {{< num ch21 campaign_reviews_per_day int >}} a day over the campaign week, against a capacity of {{< num ch21 capacity int >}}. So work that nobody chose to skip started getting skipped.

Neither problem shows in a single alert; both are obvious on a daily chart. So track three numbers weekly: the share of cases in each zone, the queue against capacity, and predicted threats against confirmed ones. When they drift apart, a person chooses a response: refit calibration on the latest week, lower the act threshold for the affected kind of case for a while, or add review capacity until the campaign ends.

The purpose of a probability is an action. This chapter is the machinery for getting from one to the other without fooling yourself.

::: {.exercises}
1. Your audit checks 3% of the act zone. After four weeks, analysts have found 11 real threats among 1,200 audited alerts. Estimate the true miss rate in the act zone, and say about how uncertain that estimate is. (Hint: this is a proportion, and Chapter 2's tools are enough.)
2. Design an act/review/escalate policy for a problem outside security, such as refunds, insurance claims or content moderation. What does each door mean? Which mistake is expensive? What capacity limits the review door?
:::
